title: Tharoor Calls Dhurandhar Superb Filmmaking and Propaganda in the Same Review
excerpt: The Congress MP praised the Ranveer Singh franchise's craft across eight hours, then faulted its politics and called its violence among the most disgusting scenes ever seen in Indian cinema.
body:
• Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, reviewing both Dhurandhar films in a video on his YouTube channel, called the sequel superb filmmaking and, in the same breath, propaganda with excessive violence.
  • He described some scenes as among the most disgusting ever seen in Indian cinema, while praising the acting, sets, design and direction across the two films' eight hours.
  • The Aditya Dhar franchise, led by Ranveer Singh, has collected more than Rs 3,100 crore worldwide across its December 2025 and March 2026 instalments.
  • Tharoor noted bans in Pakistan and several Gulf countries, and wondered how Pakistani viewers would read a film he says shows them how much wrong has been done in their name.

Shashi Tharoor has done something few politicians attempt with a blockbuster: reviewed it properly. After watching both parts of Aditya Dhar's Dhurandhar, the Congress MP posted a video on his official YouTube channel that praises the filmmaking in terms most critics would envy, then faults the franchise for propaganda and for violence he calls totally excessive.

"As a work of fiction, as a work of entertainment, there is no doubt that the second part is superb," Tharoor said, in comments reported by Hungama Express. He said he enjoyed the second instalment, Dhurandhar: The Revenge, more than the first.

Praise First, and It Is Not Faint

Tharoor's verdict on the craft is unambiguous. "Vividly made, bound to have an impact on anyone who has an imagination or a mind. Competent acting, superb sort of sets, design, and direction. At the end of 8 hours, you feel you have been through a major cinematic experience," he said.

The numbers support the scale of that experience. The two films, released in December 2025 and March 2026 and starring Ranveer Singh alongside Akshaye Khanna, R. Madhavan, Sanjay Dutt, Arjun Rampal and Rakesh Bedi, have collectively earned more than Rs 3,100 crore worldwide, making the spy franchise one of the biggest commercial successes in Indian cinema history.

The Violence Objection

"There was no need to show so much violence, blood, mayhem, cruelty and some of the most disgusting scenes ever seen in Indian cinema."

— Shashi Tharoor, Congress MP

Tharoor's sharpest criticism was reserved for the gore. He called the graphic violence totally excessive and over the top, arguing the story could have been told without scenes of that intensity. It is a criticism other reviewers have made of the franchise, but it carries different weight from a parliamentarian who is himself a prolific author and a regular voice in India's cultural debates.

The Propaganda Question

On the charge that has followed the films since release, Tharoor did not dodge. "There is a lot of propaganda stuff built into it obviously and I gather the film has been banned in many countries, not just in Pakistan, but many of the Gulf countries have banned it, saying it would needlessly create bad blood between Indians and Pakistanis, so I can understand those feelings," he said, according to Chronica Times.

His most quoted line was about the audience the film cannot legally reach. "I don't know how Pakistanis will react if they see this. Some of the lines, I think Pakistanis will laugh. Some of the other things, I think Pakistanis will realise how much wrong has been done in their name."

Why This Review Travels

For diaspora audiences, Dhurandhar has been both a box-office event and an argument: about how Indian cinema now portrays Pakistan, about how much violence a spy thriller needs, and about where entertainment ends and messaging begins. Tharoor's review does not settle any of those arguments. It gives each side its strongest lines, in one seven-minute video, from a man whose party is in opposition to the politics the film is accused of serving.

What's Next

The franchise's commercial run is already historic. The debate Tharoor joined, over propaganda, bans and the portrayal of a neighbour, will run longer than the films themselves, and his review is now one of its reference points.
